An incredibly shrinking Firefox faces endangered species status.

I personally switched off of Firefox about a year ago because of they insisted on changing the way the browser looked without a way to keep it the same. Every update I would have to search for different extensions to undo the gui changes and finally I just gave up and switched to Palemoon. It's done fine by me since the guid change that screwed things up for some extensions but after a couple of updates it's been very solid since then.

That being said, I'd probably switch back to Firefox proper before going to another browser as I've been dissatisfied with the extension options for the others compared to Firefox.

I had to bail last month for a number of reasons:

  • The layout, no matter how much I use the customise button, changes a lot with updates - buttons come and go etc. I spend too much time tweaking this.
  • Sync is not a good experience, especially on Linux where it keeps signing me out.
  • Also I was pissed when they basically killed the option to host your own sync server - one of the reasons I left chrome.
  • Developing extensions for it sucks, and there's no sandboxing. This means a lot of Chromium extensions can do things that would be insecure on FF.
  • FF for Android is one of my favourite browsers on mobile, but because sync is no good it quickly feels a little broken. I can see how they are at a disadvantage here though - it's not easy competing with Google on their own platform.

I like to use open source projects where I can and I admire the work Mozilla is trying to do, but I just can't use Firefox full time anymore. There are niggles with Chromium, but the pros outway the cons right now.

A more personal reason is the ease of account switching. We use Google Apps at work and I use a few Google things myself, Chromium makes switching between the two easy, and keeps them well away from each other - extensions and all.

I run Firefox on my PC because of noscript and adblock plus. I haven't seen an as effective combination on other browser platforms, although I do admit it's been some 6 - 12 months since I last looked around. FF on my android is great, I don't know what the problem is.
Adblockplus is on chrome, and Chrome has noscript-style features built into the browser - if that's insufficient, there's also extensions such as Scriptno or HTTP Dashboard that do the same thing.
I don't use Firefox due to its lack of touch support. It's pretty much useless on a touch device.

They don't seem to respond to their users. I just want a "task manager" and sandboxing. i'm still using ff on one of my 3 daily used computers and after using it for a while "something" will peg the cpu. I go through and close each tab watching the usage and it doesn't change, so i have to turn it off and back on. but, even though the window closes it takes quite a while for the program to close, which is also annoying. All of these have been problems that i've had for years now, and i'm not the only one.

The whole thing feels like shuttleworth's insistence on unity and the way unity was going to work, even though the community overall hated it, and it diverted resources from making the os more stable (what would actually attract people to ubuntu).

Also, keep an eye on vivaldi, it is really nice and can use chrome's extensions. If it keeps progressing as it has been i think the next exodus might be their way (firefox -> chrome -> vivaldi).

Vivaldi's problem is that it claims to be all about customization but then literally offers less customization options than Sleipnir or Chromium, and it subscribes to Opera's cancerous UI layout.

It has the potential to be something good in a few years but right now it's garbage.
I've used FF as my main browser for over 5 years yet I've recently switched to IceCat. Has the same privacy-minded addons that FF has, yet runs way faster. And FOSS.
As much as I love Firefox on my desktop, I really dislike the mobile version.

I see a lot of PaleMoon support in here. Personally I use both interchangeably to hold different identities as well as different add-ons and settings. It's quite curious that Chrome still has such a large market share as the browser's been quite a memory hog for the past couple years.

Personally my not too distant browser history starts off with Firefox and moved to Chrome due to many features didn't need add-ons installed. This meant that I could have an even more customized experience and not have to worry about continually reloading it on a new install. Bittorrent Sync makes the transfer all that more smooth.
